meta.blurb: One man working alone could scarcely make a single pin in a day. Ten men sharing the work made over 48,000. In 1776 Adam Smith used this small workshop to ask why some nations grow rich and others stay poor.
meta.bible: Adam Smith: Scottish thinker, born in Kirkcaldy in 1723, professor at Glasgow, died in Edinburgh in 1790; he never married. The Wealth of Nations: his great book, published in March 1776, in five parts called books; its full title is An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations. The Theory of Moral Sentiments: his first book, 1759. Kirkcaldy: his home town in Scotland. Glasgow: where he taught. Edinburgh: where he was a commissioner of customs from 1778. Scotland. Britain. London. Leith. America: the British colonies. Parliament. East India Company: a powerful trading company with a monopoly. Navigation Act: a British law about shipping. Corn Laws: British taxes on imported grain, repealed in 1846. David Ricardo, Karl Marx, John Maynard Keynes: later economists. Fixed facts: ten men in a small pin workshop shared about eighteen tasks and made more than 48,000 pins a day; one man alone could scarcely make twenty. Smith used the phrase invisible hand once in this book. The wine example says wine in Scotland would cost about thirty times as much. Voice and tone: clear, curious and fair, explaining one idea at a time with everyday examples; where Smith was disputed or later economists disagreed, say so plainly.

B1B2: In 1776 a Scottish thinker named Adam Smith published a long book about money and work. He wanted to know why some nations grow rich while others stay poor.
Smith did not think that wealth meant piles of gold and silver. He believed it was the food, clothes and tools that a nation's people make and use every year.
Smith begins his book with something small, the making of a pin. He says that one man, working alone and without training, could hardly make one pin in a day, and certainly not twenty.

Smith had seen a small workshop where ten men shared the work, one drawing the wire and another straightening it. Between them they did about eighteen separate jobs, and together they made more than 48,000 pins in a day.
Smith gives three reasons why dividing the work makes it more productive. A worker who repeats one job becomes skilful, wastes no time moving between tasks, and may invent a better tool for it.
In the first steam engines, a boy had to open and close a valve again and again. One boy wanted to play with his friends, so he tied a string to the handle and let the machine do the work.
Think of the plain woollen coat that an ordinary working man wears in winter. Smith pointed out that shepherds, spinners, weavers, sailors and many others all had a part in making it.
Smith did not think that people ever planned to divide up their work. He said it grew from the human habit of swapping one thing for another, which no dog has ever shown.
Smith wrote that we get our dinner from the butcher, the brewer and the baker. They do not provide it out of kindness, he said, but because they want to earn a living.
Smith asked why a scholar and a street porter seem so different. He thought they were much alike as small children, and that habit and education made most of the difference.
Smith said that the division of labour depends on how many buyers a trader can reach. Towns on the sea and on rivers grew rich first, because a ship carries far more goods than a wagon.

Swapping goods directly is awkward, because the baker may not want what the shoemaker has to offer. So many societies found something that everyone would accept, and in the end most chose metals like gold and silver.
Smith said that the real price of anything is the work it takes to get it, not the money paid. A loaf is dear when it costs a great deal of toil and cheap when it costs only a little.

Smith said that every good has a natural price, which pays for the wages, profit and rent that went into making it. The market price rises when goods are scarce and falls when they are plentiful, yet it is always drawn back towards the natural price.
Smith said that wages come from a bargain between workers and masters, who want opposite things. Masters find it easier to act together than workers do, and the law of his day was kinder to them.
Smith did not think high wages were a problem for a country. He said that well-paid workers are healthier and more active, and that no society can flourish when most of its people are poor.
Smith said that all the income of a nation is shared in three ways. Workers receive wages, the owners of money and tools receive profit, and the owners of land receive rent.
In the second part of the book, Smith explains what he calls stock, which we now call capital. It is the part of a person's goods that is kept back, not to be used today, but to earn a profit.
Smith saw that banks could lend paper notes instead of gold coins. He compared this to building a road through the air, since it freed a costly stock of gold for better use.
Smith believed that a nation grows richer when people save part of their income. The money that is saved does not vanish, because it is used to pay workers and buy tools.

Smith divided work into two kinds, and he thought only one kind adds to a nation's wealth. A carpenter who makes chairs adds value, in his view, while a servant's work vanishes at the moment it is done, and later economists disagreed.
The third part of the book looks at how nations grow rich step by step. The natural order, he said, is to improve farms first, because towns live on the food that farms provide.
Smith said that Europe followed a different path after the Roman Empire fell. Great lords owned huge estates, and it was the towns that slowly brought back trade and order.

The fourth part of the book attacks the mercantile system, which was the usual thinking of rulers in Smith's day. It said that a country grows rich by selling more than it buys and by keeping the gold.
Smith said that money is only a tool for moving goods from one person to another. A country with plenty of gold but few goods is still poor, whatever its treasure rooms may hold.
Smith said that the purpose of making goods is for people to use them. Yet the laws of his day protected sellers and made ordinary buyers pay more, which seemed upside down to him.

Smith pointed out that good grapes could be grown in Scotland under glass and beside heated walls. The wine would cost about thirty times as much as wine from abroad, so it would be foolish to forbid people to buy foreign wine.
Smith wrote that a sensible head of a family never makes at home what costs less to buy. The tailor buys his shoes from the shoemaker, and the shoemaker buys his coat from the tailor.
Smith wrote that a merchant who invests his money at home usually thinks only of his own gain. Yet he is led, as if by an invisible hand, to help society, although that was never his aim.

When harvests were bad, angry crowds often blamed the corn dealers. Smith argued that dealers actually helped, because they spread the scarce grain over the whole year, and that laws against them made things worse.
Smith did not claim that every rule about trade was a mistake. He approved of the Navigation Act, which helped British sailors and ships, because he judged that defence matters more than wealth.
Britain forced its colonies in America to trade mainly through Britain. Smith said this hurt both sides, and he suggested that the colonists should send members to Parliament.
Smith disliked companies like the East India Company, which had a legal monopoly on trade. Their managers, he said, handle other people's money and seldom guard it as carefully as their own.
Smith warned that people in the same trade seldom meet without talking about how to raise prices. For this reason, he said, a new law proposed by merchants should always be examined with great care.
The fifth and last book asks what a government should do and what it should pay for. The first duty, he said, is defence, and in a modern state war is a skill that needs trained soldiers.
Smith named justice as the second duty of the state. He argued that judges should be independent of the ruler, so that every person feels safe from wrong and can trust the law.

Smith said that a government should build roads, bridges and harbours that help trade but that private people would not build. He thought that the people who use them should pay for them through tolls.

Smith saw one danger in the division of labour, which is that doing one small task all day can dull a person's mind. To protect workers, he said, the public should help to pay for schools where children learn to read, write and count.
Smith set out four rules, or maxims, that every good tax should follow. It should be fair to people's means, certain and clear, convenient for the person who pays, and cheap to collect.
Smith did not think that taxes had to be exactly equal in size. He wrote that it was not unreasonable for the rich to pay a little more than their share, for example higher tolls on fine carriages.

In wartime, Smith noticed, governments find it easier to borrow than to raise taxes, and they seldom repay in full. He warned that when such debts grow very large, they can weaken a nation for a long time.
Near the end, Smith told Britain to be realistic about its empire. If the colonies would not share the cost, he said, Britain should fit its plans to its real means.

Adam Smith was born in Kirkcaldy, Scotland, in 1723, and he later became a professor at Glasgow. He spent about ten years writing this book, after an earlier one called The Theory of Moral Sentiments.
The first edition sold out in about six months, and four more editions followed in Smith's lifetime. In 1778 he became a customs commissioner in Edinburgh, and he died there in 1790.
Some people think that Smith simply praised selfishness, but his other book shows otherwise. In it he wrote that people care about others, feel sympathy, and want to be admired for good conduct.
Many economists after Smith built on his work, among them David Ricardo. Others, such as Karl Marx and later John Maynard Keynes, challenged parts of it, and the debate goes on today.
Smith's arguments for free trade had a great influence on later reformers in Britain. In 1846 Britain repealed the Corn Laws, which had kept the price of bread high by taxing imported grain.
Think of a modern phone, made from parts and materials that come from many countries. Smith's pin workshop has grown into a worldwide chain of workers, and nobody alone could make the whole phone.
Smith trusted markets, but he did not trust monopolies or special favours. He wanted fair courts, good roads and schools, because a free market needs a society that works well around it.
The lesson of Smith's book is simple: a nation is rich when its ordinary people can eat, dress and live well. That comes from skilled work shared among many hands, in a society that is free and fair.
C1C2: When Adam Smith published his great book in March 1776, few readers could have guessed how long it would shape the way people think about money. Its full title promised an inquiry into the nature and causes of the wealth of nations, and it kept that promise across two thick volumes. Smith wanted to explain why some countries grow prosperous while others remain poor, and he set out to answer in plain, patient prose.

Many people in Smith's day believed that a rich nation was one with a great store of gold and silver in its treasury. Smith disagreed, and he argued that real wealth is the yearly flow of food, clothing and useful goods that a people produces and enjoys. By that measure, a country was richer when its ordinary families lived better, whatever its vaults might hold.

Smith opens his argument with a humble example, the making of a common pin, and he asks the reader to picture one worker doing every task alone. Such a man, untrained in the trade and without the right tools, could hardly make a single pin in a day, and certainly could not make twenty. The example looks trivial, yet it holds the central idea of the whole book, which is that shared work can multiply what people are able to make.

Smith then describes a small workshop he had seen, where ten men shared the work of making pins, one drawing out the wire, another straightening it, a third cutting it and others sharpening and polishing. About eighteen separate operations were divided among them, so that each man became expert in only a small part of the whole. Together, he reports, they could make more than 48,000 pins in a day, which came to about 4,800 pins for each man, far more than any lone worker could dream of making.

Smith traced the gain to three separate causes, all of which can be seen in a workshop of any kind. A man who repeats one simple task all day grows wonderfully quick and skilful at it, and he no longer wastes the time that is lost in passing from one job to another. Because his whole attention rests on a single operation, he is also the likeliest person to notice a machine that would make the work easier.

Smith liked to show that useful ideas often come from the people who do the work. In the earliest steam engines a boy was kept busy opening and closing a valve at the proper moment, and one of them, eager to go and play, tied a string from the valve handle to another moving part. The engine then did the task by itself and the boy was free, which Smith offered as a small proof that ordinary workers invent improvements.

Smith asked his readers to look at the rough woollen coat of a common day-labourer, which seems to be a very simple thing. Yet the shepherd, the wool-sorter, the spinner, the weaver, the dyer and the sailor who carried the goods all had a share in making it, along with many others. Even the poorest person in a civilised country, he concluded, is helped by the work of thousands of people he will never meet.

Where, Smith asked, does the division of labour come from, and who first decided that people should divide their work? He answered that it grew slowly out of a human habit, the tendency to truck, barter and exchange one thing for another, rather than out of any wise plan. No one has ever seen a dog make a fair and deliberate swap of one bone for another with a second dog, he noted, and that is a difference between us and the animals.

Smith made one of his most famous points about trade by using three ordinary shopkeepers from any town as his example. It is not from the kindness of the butcher, the brewer or the baker that we expect our dinner, he wrote, but from their regard for their own interest. We do not appeal to their generosity, he said, but speak to their self-love, and we talk to them of their gain rather than of our own needs.

Smith did not believe that people are born with very different talents, whatever the habits of society may suggest. A philosopher and a common street porter, he suggested, are probably much alike when they are small children, and what separates them later is largely habit, custom and education. It was the division of labour itself, he said, that pushed them into different trades and so made their abilities seem so unequal.

Smith saw that the division of labour has a limit, and that limit is the size of the market, for no one will specialise in a trade if there are too few buyers. He observed that a wagon with two men and eight horses carried about four tons between London and Edinburgh in six weeks, while a ship with a few sailors could carry some two hundred tons in the same time. For that reason, he noted, trade and skill first flourished along coasts and navigable rivers.

Smith imagined how money must have begun, for swapping goods directly works badly when the butcher wants bread but the baker has no wish for meat. People therefore tried various things that everyone would accept, including salt, cattle, dried fish and tobacco, in different times and places. In the end, he said, metals won out because they last, can be divided and are easily carried, and so coins appeared.

Smith insisted that the true price of any good is not the number of coins it costs but the toil and trouble of acquiring it, since labour was the first price paid for everything. Money, he said, is only a convenient measure, and its value can rise or fall as mines are found and silver becomes common. Labour alone, he argued, never changes in its own worth to the worker, who gives up the same ease, liberty and happiness each time.

Smith distinguished between the natural price of a good, which just covers the wages, profit and rent needed to bring it to market, and its market price, which is what it actually sells for on a given day. When goods are scarce the market price climbs above the natural one, and when they are plentiful it sinks below it. Because buyers, sellers and producers respond to these signals, he said, the price is constantly pulled back toward the natural level.

Smith noted that wages are settled by a bargain between workers, who wish to get as much as they can, and masters, who wish to give as little as possible. The masters, being few and wealthy, could hold out longer and combine more easily, and the laws of the time forbade combinations of workmen while hardly noticing those of employers. In this struggle, he admitted, the advantage usually lay quite plainly with the masters rather than with the men.

Unlike many writers of his time, Smith welcomed high wages, which he took as the clearest sign of a nation whose wealth was growing. A workman who is well fed and decently paid, he argued, becomes more active, more diligent and more hopeful than one who is kept hungry. No society can be flourishing and happy, he said, when most of its members are poor, and it is only fair that those who feed and clothe the nation be decently fed themselves.

In Smith's account, the income of a nation is divided into three great streams, each belonging to a different class of people. The labourer earns wages, the owner of capital earns profit on the stock he has risked, and the owner of land receives rent for letting others farm it. These three groups, he thought, made up the body of society, and their interests were not always the same.

In the second book, Smith turned to stock, which we would now call capital, meaning the goods that a person keeps not for immediate use but to earn an income. He divided it into fixed capital, such as machines and buildings that bring a profit while staying in the same hands, and circulating capital, such as materials that bring a profit only when sold. A farmer's plough, for example, belongs to the first kind, and his seed-corn to the second.

Smith was impressed by the banks of Scotland, whose paper notes let merchants trade without carrying heavy coin. He compared the change to building a wagon-way through the air, since the gold and silver that no longer had to circulate could be put to work elsewhere, like a road turned into a cornfield. He also warned, however, that banks which lend too freely can create dangers for themselves and for the public.

According to Smith, it is saving, rather than industry alone, that makes the capital of a nation grow, since work can only gather together what thrift has put aside. The frugal man, he said, is a public benefactor, because what he saves is soon spent in hiring working people. The spendthrift, by contrast, eats up in idle pleasures the very funds that might have given work to others.

In one of his more disputed passages, Smith distinguished productive labour, which fixes itself in a good that can be sold, from unproductive labour, which perishes at the moment it is performed. A weaver's cloth belonged to the first sort, while the work of a servant, a soldier or even a king fell, in his scheme, into the second. Later economists found this line hard to defend, and most today would count services among the things that a nation produces.

In the third book Smith asked in what order a nation would grow rich if nothing interfered with its progress. The natural course, he answered, begins on the land, for people must be fed before they can be clothed or housed, and only a surplus of food from the countryside can support a town. The town in turn sends back manufactured goods, so that country and town each feed the other's prosperity.

Europe, Smith argued, followed this natural course in reverse, for after the fall of Rome its lands were held in vast estates by lords whose power rested on armed followers. Towns became the first places where trade and ordinary law could grow, and the merchants who lived there slowly changed the countryside around them. In the end the great lords gave up their power over their tenants in exchange for fine goods to wear and show, and so, without ever intending it, they helped to bring about a freer society.

The fourth book turns to what Smith called the mercantile system, the doctrine that guided most European governments of his day. Its supporters held that a nation grows rich by selling more to foreigners than it buys from them, so that gold and silver flow in and are kept at home. Smith meant to show that this idea was mistaken, and that it did real harm to the people who lived under it.

To Smith, gold and silver were merely the wheels of trade, valuable for what they can buy and for nothing more, and a nation could not become rich by hoarding them. A country with full warehouses, busy farms and skilled workers is wealthy even if its treasury is thin, while one that has only a heap of coin and few useful goods is poor. Besides, he reasoned, rules meant to trap gold inside a country rarely work, because money flows to wherever goods are wanted.

Everything produced, Smith insisted, is made in the end for someone to consume, and the interest of the maker matters only so far as it serves the buyer. The mercantile laws turned this upside down, he said, because duties and bans on foreign goods helped a few well-organised producers while every other family paid higher prices. It seemed to him a plain case of the many being made to serve the few.

Smith offered a vivid example of foolish policy, and he took it from the cold and rainy climate of his native Scotland. With glass, hotbeds and heated walls, he said, good grapes and even good wine could be produced in Scotland, though at about thirty times the cost of equally good wine brought in from abroad. To forbid the import of foreign wine so that Scots might make their own would plainly be absurd, and the same reasoning, he added, holds for every trade between nations.

Smith appealed to common sense in the practice of every careful household, which never tries to make at home what would cost more to make than to buy. The tailor does not stitch his own shoes, nor does the shoemaker sew his own coat, because each finds it better to use his skill where it counts most and to buy the rest. What is sensible in a private family, Smith concluded, can hardly be foolish in a great kingdom.

In a famous passage, Smith wrote that a merchant who prefers to invest his money at home intends only his own security and gain. Yet in this, as in many other cases, he is led by an invisible hand to promote an end that was no part of his intention. Smith used the phrase only once in this book, and it is still debated today how much weight he meant it to carry.

When harvests failed, hungry crowds in Smith's time often blamed the corn dealers and demanded that the law restrain them. Smith argued that the dealer, in seeking his profit, does the public a service by making the scarce grain last through the whole year instead of being used up in the first months. Laws against his trade, he believed, were born of popular fear and tended to turn a hard year into a famine.

Smith was not an absolute opponent of all rules, and he admitted that a few were wise. The Navigation Act, which required that goods be carried in British ships, was in his view justified, because a strong fleet and a body of trained seamen were vital to the safety of the island. Defence, he said bluntly, is of much more importance than wealth, and a nation must sometimes pay a price for it.

Smith wrote his book while Britain and its American colonies drifted into war, and he turned a critical eye on the trade laws that forced colonists to buy and sell mainly through Britain. These laws, he argued, held back the colonies and also cost British consumers dearly, in order to enrich a handful of merchants at home. As a remedy, he proposed that the colonies should be given seats in Parliament in proportion to the taxes they paid, so that the empire might become one united state.

Smith had little faith in the great trading companies of his day, of which the East India Company was the most powerful, because the law gave them a monopoly and shielded them from competition. Their directors, he observed, were managers of other people's money, and could hardly be expected to watch over it with the same anxious care as partners watch over their own. The result, he thought, was a good deal of carelessness and waste, which the public had to pay for.

Smith was no flatterer of business people, and he remarked that those in the same trade seldom meet, even for pleasure, without the talk turning to some scheme for raising prices. When merchants and manufacturers propose a new law, he said, the public should examine it long and carefully, with the most suspicious attention. Their interest, he noted, is never exactly the same as the interest of the public, and it often runs against it.

The fifth book asks what a government should do and how it should pay for it, and Smith began with the oldest duty of all, which is to defend the society from violence and invasion. He argued that as nations grow rich and their people become absorbed in their trades, war turns into a specialised art, so that a standing army of professional soldiers is better than part-time fighters. Even here, then, he applied his favourite principle, that work is done best when it is divided among those trained for it.

The second duty of the sovereign, in Smith's view, is to protect every member of society from the injustice and oppression of every other, which means setting up an exact system of justice. He argued that the judges should be independent of the government, because people can feel secure in their property and their persons only when they trust the courts to be fair. Without such trust, he implied, patient work and long-term saving would hardly seem worthwhile to anyone, and trade would wither.

The third duty, Smith said, is to raise and maintain those public works that serve a whole society but that no private person would find profitable to build, such as roads, bridges, canals and harbours. He preferred that they be paid for by the people who actually use them, through tolls, rather than by general taxes that fall on those who never travel by them. Good roads, he noted, bring distant markets nearer, and so they widen the division of labour.

Smith was honest about one cost of the division of labour, for a man who spends his life on a few simple operations has little chance to use his understanding. He feared that such a worker might become as dull and ignorant as a human being can be, and his remedy was education. He proposed that the public should help to support small schools where the children of working families could learn to read, write and keep accounts.

In his long discussion of taxes, Smith laid down four maxims that are still quoted today. A tax should be fair, taking from each person according to his ability to pay, and it should be certain, so that nobody is left to the whim of the collector. It should also be levied at a time and in a manner convenient to the payer, and it should cost little to collect, so that as much as possible reaches the public treasury.

Smith had no objection to asking the wealthy for something more than a strict proportion of their income. He remarked that it was not very unreasonable for the rich to contribute to public costs in proportion to their means and a little beyond, and he suggested higher tolls on luxury carriages. In this way, he wrote, the vanity of the rich would be made to lighten the cost of carrying heavy goods for everybody else.

Smith observed that governments, when they go to war, find it easier to borrow than to raise taxes, and so debts grow with every campaign. When such debts have once reached a great size, he warned, there is scarcely a single case of their being fairly paid, and nations have usually escaped them by some kind of cheating. Britain's own debt, which had swollen during its wars, filled him with real alarm about the future.

Smith closed his enormous book with advice that no government of his day wished to hear. If the American colonies would not help to pay for the empire, he said, then Britain ought to let them go and adapt her future views and designs to the real mediocrity of her circumstances. It was a sober ending to a book that had begun with something as small as a pin.

Adam Smith was born in 1723 in the Scottish port of Kirkcaldy, studied at Glasgow and Oxford, and taught moral philosophy at the University of Glasgow. His first book, The Theory of Moral Sentiments, appeared in 1759 and made him famous, and he then spent about ten years, much of them in quiet study, on the book that is now remembered as his masterpiece. He never married, and he lived a modest, studious life among his books and his friends.

The book was an immediate success, for the first edition sold out in about six months and four more editions appeared while its author was still alive. In 1778 Smith accepted a post as a commissioner of customs in Edinburgh, which gave him a steady income and a close view of the very tariffs he had criticised. He died there in 1790, honoured across Europe, having asked his friends to burn most of his unpublished papers.

It is sometimes said that Smith praised selfishness, yet that picture does not survive a reading of his other book, in which sympathy, fairness and conscience stand at the centre of human life. For him, self-interest was one strong motive among several, useful in the market but never a complete account of how people ought to behave. He wanted the market to serve a decent society, and he criticised employers and merchants who tried to use it against ordinary people.

Economists of the nineteenth century, led by David Ricardo, took up Smith's ideas and made them more exact, while Karl Marx used some of them to argue against capitalism itself. In the twentieth century John Maynard Keynes challenged the belief that markets always cure themselves without help from governments. Nearly every school of economics since then has had to explain how it agrees or differs with the book of 1776.

The case that Smith made against trade restrictions gradually won over British politicians and the public, and it helped to inspire the campaign for free trade in the nineteenth century. In 1846 Britain repealed the Corn Laws, which had kept the price of bread high by taxing imported grain, and for several decades afterwards it led the world in lowering tariffs. Smith, who had been dead for more than half a century by then, had finally been given his victory.

Smith's pin workshop has grown into a worldwide network, for the phone in a modern hand contains materials mined, refined, shaped and assembled by many thousands of people in dozens of countries. None of them could make the whole device alone, and few of them will ever meet. The coat of the day-labourer that Smith described has become a far larger and more astonishing miracle of cooperation.

Read as a whole, the book is neither a simple hymn to the market nor an attack on governments. Smith trusted free exchange to do far more than rulers could achieve by command, yet he also wanted fair courts, strong defence, useful roads and schools, and he distrusted every monopoly and special privilege. His ideal was a system of natural liberty in which a just state protects everyone's right to work and trade.

In the end, the lesson of The Wealth of Nations is that a country is rich not when its treasury is full but when its ordinary families are well fed, well clothed and secure. Such prosperity grows from work that is divided and exchanged freely, from savings that are put to good use, and from a government that keeps order without choking enterprise. Smith's humble pin has become a measure for all of us, because it shows how much more we can achieve together than any of us can achieve alone.
